nameStory: The gray hairstreak gets its name from the delicate, hair-thin tails that extend from its hindwings, looking like wispy strands streaming behind it in flight. The 'gray' refers to the subtle blue-gray coloring on the undersides of its wings, though this common butterfly is anything but dull when you look closely.
description: The gray hairstreak is a small, active butterfly with a wingspan of about 1 to 1.5 inches. It belongs to the gossamer-winged butterfly family, named for their delicate, almost translucent wing texture. The wings are typically gray-brown above and lighter blue-gray below, with distinctive orange spots and thin 'tails' on the hindwings. This is one of the most common and widespread hairstreaks in North America, making it a great butterfly for beginners to learn.

idTips.label: Hair-like wing tails
idTips.description: Look for the characteristic thin, thread-like projections extending from the hindwings - they feel delicate and may flutter independently in a breeze

idTips.label: Orange eyespots
idTips.description: Bright orange or red-orange spots near the wing tails on the underside, often with a small black dot in the center

idTips.label: Blue-gray underside
idTips.description: Wings underneath have a soft, powdery blue-gray appearance with a fine white line running across both wings

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: About the size of a quarter when wings are spread, with a quick, darting flight pattern close to the ground

idTips.label: Wing position at rest
idTips.description: Always holds wings vertically above its body when landed, never spreading them flat like many other butterflies

idTips.label: Antenna clubs
idTips.description: Short antennae with distinct rounded clubs at the tips, often with white markings on the club ends

habitat: Gray hairstreaks are incredibly adaptable and can be found in almost any open, sunny area including gardens, parks, roadsides, fields, and forest edges throughout New England. They particularly favor areas with legume plants like clover, beans, and wild lupine, as well as flowering shrubs and trees. Look for them from sea level to moderate elevations, wherever there are flowers to nectar on and host plants for their caterpillars.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with fresh individuals appearing in May. Look for them nectaring on early wildflowers and fruit tree blossoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August, with multiple generations flying. This is the best time to observe their courtship behaviors and egg-laying.
seasonality.fall: Still active through September and early October, with the final generation preparing for winter. Adults may appear more worn and faded.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as a chrysalis (pupa) hidden in leaf litter or attached to host plants. No adults are active during winter months.

funFact: Gray hairstreak caterpillars are agricultural shape-shifters - they can eat over 40 different plant families and will actually change color to match their food, turning pink on hibiscus, green on beans, or even white on cotton, earning them the alternate name 'cotton square borer.'
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other hairstreak species, but gray hairstreaks are typically the most common and have the most subdued coloring. Remember 'gray is the gateway' - if you're seeing your first hairstreak, it's probably this species since it's so widespread and numerous.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'bean lycaenid' and 'cotton square borer,' gray hairstreaks are rarely serious agricultural pests since their populations are naturally controlled by predators and they prefer wild plants over crops in most situations.
compareHints: As the only Strymon species commonly found in New England, gray hairstreaks are most similar to other hairstreak butterflies in the gossamer-wing family. However, they're generally less colorful than species like the banded hairstreak (which has more pronounced white stripes) and larger than the tiny copper butterflies. Their gray coloring and widespread abundance make them the 'default' hairstreak in most New England locations.
